articles.title: Dogmatic Bayesianism Disorder
articles.content:
Note: This humorously intended sarcastic blog post directly mimics classifications of psychological disorders in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of the American Psychological Association, but Dogmatic Bayesianism is not in the DSM-5 as an actual psychological disorder - for now.

 

Dogmatic Bayesianism Disorder

Diagnostic Criteria                                              F61.1

A. Individuals are convinced that they know what other people want to know.

 

B. Individuals believe that everyone who is not a Bayesian is wrong. They almost continuously try to convince others, and there is often a strong feeling others need to be ‘saved’.

 

C. Strong tendency to ridicule non-Bayesians, including historical figures. Karl Popper (who opposed Bayesianism, as it opens the door to dogmatism in science) is an especially common target.

 

D. A pervasive obsession with Bayesian statistics, and the use of p-values or hypothesis testing by others, at the expense of flexibility, openness, and acknowledging that other coherent statistical approaches exist to deal with uncertainty.

 

E. Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning. The forceful insertion of Bayesian statistics into conversations can drive away conversation partners, to the point where almost all social contact is restricted to other dogmatic Bayesians.

 

F. Individuals believe everyone else will become a Bayesian. Older dogmatic Bayesian often lose bets that everyone will have become a Bayesian by a specific year. If this bet is lost, they continue to claim everyone will become a Bayesian in the future and consider this a rationally updated belief.

 

Specify if:

Persistent: The disorder has been present for more than 12 months.

Specify current severity:

Dogmatic Bayesianism Disorder is specified as severe when an academic exhibits all symptoms of the disorder, at which point individuals are classified as having Bayesian Evangelical Syndrome (BES).

 

Prevalence

Less than 0.01% of the general population is affected, but prevalence is estimated to be at 1% to 2% in statistically inclined academics. Due to diagnostic criterion E prevalence can be up to 80% on certain internet forums. Men are more frequently affected than women, at a ratio estimated at 100:1 or greater.  

Development and course

Development of the condition often starts in the early thirties, but onset can occur at an older age, in which case the symptoms are often much more severe. There is currently no treatment, and dogmatic Bayesianism typically increases with age. In rare cases (less than 1%) spontaneous recovery seems to occur, after which individuals often experience prolonged feelings of shame and embarrassment.

Risk and Prognostic Factors

The disorder is more common in individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

articles.title: On the reliability and reproducibility of qualitative research
articles.content:
With my collaborators, I am increasingly performing qualitative research. I find qualitative research projects a useful way to improve my understanding of behaviors that I want to explore with other methods in the future. For example, some years ago I performed qualitative interviews with researchers who believed their own research had no value whatsoever. Although I did not intend to publish these interviews, they provided important insights for other projects that I am engaged in now. I was involved in qualitative research on the assessment process of interdisciplinary research (Schölvinck et al., 2024), and we performed interviews to understand how researchers interpret a questionnaire we were developing that measures personal values in science (Kis et al., 2025). Together with Anna van ‘Veer I supervised Julia Weschenfelder who interviewed scientists on what they believed the value of their research was, and I have hired Julia as a PhD as part of a large project on the meaningful interpretation of effect sizes. She is planning interviews with researchers about what determined the maximum sample size they are willing to collect (if you want to be interviewed about this, reach out!). With Sajedeh Rasti, who is completing her PhD in my lab, we have spent the last 2 years interviewing people who played important roles in the creation of large-scale coordinated research projects in science.

As a supervisor, I am always very actively involved in research projects, and I joined as many of the (extremely interesting) interviews Sajedeh performed, and I listened to the audio recordings of all interviews that Julia performed to give my interpretation of what the scientists discussed when interviewed. Yet it never occurred to me to independently perform the thematic analysis for these interviews, and compare the themes we derived. I became aware of this peculiarity after reading a great qualitative paper analyzing open questions in a study on questionable research practices (Makel et al., 2025). In this paper, two teams independently analyze themes in the same set of open questions. They largely find the same themes, and conclude: “our two independent analysis teams reported themes that were generally similar or overlapping, suggesting a robustness of the findings. We believe this suggests that independent qualitative analyst teams with similar positionality can use unique analytic paths and reach largely similar destinations. This contributes to the ongoing conversation within the qualitative research community about whether reproducibility and replicability are relevant or possible in qualitative research”.


Sometimes you read a paper that makes perfect sense – of course two independent teams should reach the same conclusions when they qualitatively analyze the same data – and yet, it was not part of your workflow. This is especially peculiar, because we use this exact workflow when we code other data sources. For example, Sajedeh Rasti will soon share a preprint on papers written by large teams of scientists. In this paper, we classify these papers into different categories, depending on the interdependencies that require coordination (e.g., epistemic, logistical, financial, etc., see Rasti et al., 2025). Sajedeh and I double-coded papers, and we discussed our levels of agreement. This is the normal thing to do. It is strange that I never considered the same approach when the data comes from interviews.

 

Research on inter-rater reliability of thematic coding

I looked into the literature to search for papers similar to Makel et al., 2025, where the same qualitative data is analyzed by multiple coders to examine how reproducible the themes are that are identified in the data. There are many more papers than the few I will list here, and someone should write a paper summarizing this literature. But this is a Sunday morning blog post, and not a systematic review, so I will just present some papers that I found interesting.

Armstrong and colleagues had six researchers independently analyze the same single focus‑group transcript, and found “close agreement on the basic themes,” but substantial divergence in how those themes were interpreted and organized, with each analyst having “‘packaged’ the themes differently.” (Armstrong et al., 1997). The authors in this paper then go on and say these differences demonstrate the inherent subjectivity in qualitative research. But this is not the message I take away from this paper at all. All coders of any type of data will differ slightly in the details they highlight. What matters most in this project is not how in verbal summaries of the themes, researchers highlight different details – that is to be expected, but also largely irrelevant – but that there is such clear agreement on the themes identified. If I read the examples in the paper, the differences are mainly in detail, where some summarize the themes at a higher level, and others on a more detailed level. Those who summarize the themes at a detailed level will of course pick out specific details others did not mention – but this can easily be improved upon by instructing coders better about the level of detail at which results should be provided, and how details should be chosen in verbal summaries.

Campbell and colleagues (2013) provide a great example of the work needed to reach high inter-rater reliability. They say that “Reliability is just as important for qualitative research as it is for quantitative research” and argue that replicability problems stem less from disagreement over themes per se than from “the unitization problem—that is, identifying appropriate blocks of text for a particular code or codes,” which can “wreak havoc when researchers try to establish intercoder reliability for in-depth semistructured interviews.” Using their own empirical coding exercise, they show that even with a detailed codebook, intercoder reliability remained modest (“54 percent reliability on average”), reflecting the interpretive complexity of semistructured interviews where “more than one theme and therefore more than one code may be applicable at once.” However, when disagreements were resolved through discussion, intercoder agreement rose dramatically to 96%, and 91% of initial disagreements were resolved. In my view, qualitative research is nothing special in this respect, as it is often difficult to achieve high inter-rater reliability in any coding project. For example, we have the same difficulty in reaching agreement when we code what the main hypothesis in a scientific paper is in metascientific research projects (Mesquida et al., 2025).

The importance and challenges of clear coding instructions related to text-segmentation is also discussed in a classic paper on the reliability qualitative research (MacQueen et al., 1998). Based on extensive experience with qualitative research at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, MacQueen and colleagues offer useful suggestions on creating a codebook that will lead to high reliability. Through an iterative process in which multiple coders independently code the same text, compare results, and revise definitions, they show how disagreement over themes is an indication of ambiguous codes – and not an inherent limitation of qualitative research. Reproducibility can be achieved by repeatedly checking whether coders can “apply the codes in a consistent manner” and refining the codebook until agreement is acceptable. The authors argue that we should not expect that coders will naturally “see” the same themes, but that they can code the same themes reliably if researchers use a disciplined, transparent, and collective codebook development process that supports reproducible qualitative analysis without denying its interpretive character.

A realist ontology in qualitative research

The idea of reliability, or reproducibility (the two concepts become intertwined in a lovely way in qualitative research, as the coder is the measurement device, so to say) in qualitative research emerges most naturally from a scientific realist perspective on knowledge generation. There are qualitative researchers who adopt philosophical perspectives that attempt to argue reliability and reproducibility are not relevant for qualitative research. I have engaged with these ideas a lot over the years, and find them unconvincing. Seale and Silverman (1997) push back strongly against the idea that reliability would not apply in qualitative research, and write “We believe that such a position can amount to methodological anarchy and resist this on 2 grounds. First, it simply makes no sense to argue that all knowledge and feelings are of equal weight and value. Even in everyday life, we readily sort fact from fancy. Why, therefore, should science be any different? Second, methodological anarchy offers a clearly negative message to the audiences of qualitative health research, suggesting that its proponents have given up claims to validity.”

I am personally more sympathetic to the view expressed by Popay and colleagues (1998): “On one side, there are those who argue that there is nothing unique about qualitative research and that traditional definitions of reliability, validity, objectivity, and generalizability apply across both qualitative and quantitative approaches. On the other side, there are those postmodernists who contend that there can be no criteria for judging qualitative research outcomes (Fuchs, 1993). In this radical relativist position, all criteria are doubtful and none can be privileged. However, both of these positions are unsatisfactory. The second is nihilistic and precludes any distinction based on systematic or other criteria. If the first is adopted, then, at best, qualitative research will always be seen as inferior to quantitative research. At worst, there is a danger that poor-quality qualitative research, which meets criteria inappropriate for the assessment of such evidence, will be privileged.” There are unique aspects of reliability in qualitative research, but qualitative research will not be taken seriously by the majority of scientists if researchers do not engage with reliability at all.

O’Conner and Joffe provide a useful guide on how to achieve inter-coder reliability in qualitative research in psychology, based on their own extensive experience (O’Connor & Joffe, 2020). They argue that “ICR helps qualitative research achieve this communicative function by showing the basic analytic structure has meaning that extends beyond an individual researcher. The logic is that if separate individuals converge on the same interpretation of the data, it implies “that the patterns in the latent content must be fairly robust and that if the readers themselves were to code the same content, they too would make the same judgments” (Potter & Levine-Donnerstein, 1999, p. 266).” They highlight how there are both external incentives to care about reliability (as it can function as a signal of quality) but also has direct benefits for the researchers performing the qualitative research.

If you feel similarly, and want to educate your students about qualitative methods where reliability and reproducibility are important, there is a nice paper that can be used to introduce your students to realist ontologies in qualitative research by Lourie and McPhail (2024). They note how the methodology literature in qualitative research often engages with interpretivist-constructivist approaches. Among my own collaborators, this perspective is not seen as appealing, and we prefer to build our qualitative research from a realist ontology. In this philosophy, inter-rater reliability, and reproducibility, are important aspects in knowledge generation (Seale, 1999). A good textbook on applied thematic analysis from this perspective is Applied Thematic Analysis (Guest et al., 2012).

I am very grateful to Makel and colleagues for making me realize I had overlooked the importance of independent coding of themes in qualitative research, and establish inter-rater reliability or reproducibility in qualitative research.

 

Personal take-home messages

After reflecting on this topic, there are some points that I am taking away from the work on reliability or reproducibility of thematic coding.

First, independent thematic analysis, and comparing how we code qualitative data, should be a standard practice in the qualitative studies in my lab. The suggestions by MacQueen and colleagues provide useful guidance that we should follow. There is nothing special about qualitative data sources in this respect.

Second, we already ask all participants if we can share full transcripts, and many agree. In our case, as we primarily interview scientists, so we are in the lucky position that they value transparency and data sharing, and that the content of our interviews is not particularly sensitive. Data sharing is of course not always possible. For example, in my interviews on why researchers felt their own research lacked any value whatsoever, many did continue to receive funding for this research, and they would not want their actual thoughts about their research to become public. But where possible, we should share transcripts for independent re-analysis and re-use.

Third, we should use the same techniques to increase the reliability of our claims in qualitative research, as we do in quantitative research. I recently have been annoyed by some extremely biased qualitative studies in metascience, where the researchers who performed the research clearly wanted their work to lead to a very specific outcome. It is easy to tell the story you want in qualitative research, if you reject the idea of reliability. But in my lab, we use methods that prevent us from allowing us to say what we want to be true, if we are wrong. In my current research project, I reserved 8000 euro out of the 1.5 million euro budget to hire ‘red teams’ (Lakens, 2020) to criticize the studies before we perform them. However, I had planned to only use red teams for large quantitative studies. I now think that I should also use the red teams for the qualitative studies I planned in the proposal, to make sure the coding of themes is reliable.

 

References

Campbell, J. L., Quincy, C., Osserman, J., & Pedersen, O. K. (2013). Coding In-depth Semistructured Interviews: Problems of Unitization and Intercoder Reliability and Agreement. Sociological Methods & Research, 42(3), 294–320. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124113500475

articles.title: New Papers: Optimal Filter Settings for ERP Research
articles.content:
Zhang, G., Garrett, D. R., & Luck, S. J. (in press). Optimal filters for ERP research I: A general approach for selecting filter settings. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14531 [preprint]

Zhang, G., Garrett, D. R., & Luck, S. J. (in press). Optimal filters for ERP research II: Recommended settings for seven common ERP components. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14530 [preprint]

What filter settings should you apply to your ERP data? If your filters are too weak to attenuate the noise in your data, your effects may not be statistically significant. If your filters are too strong, they may create artifactual peaks that lead you to draw bogus conclusions.

For years, I have been recommending a bandpass of 0.1–30 Hz for most cognitive and affective research in neurotypical young adults. In this kind of research, I have found that filtering from 0.1–30 Hz usually does a good job of minimizing noise while creating minimal waveform distortion.

However, this recommendation was based on a combination of informal observations from many experimental paradigms and a careful examination of a couple paradigms, so it was a bit hand-wavy. In addition, the optimal filter settings will depend on the waveshape of the ERP effects and the nature of the noise in a given study, so I couldn’t make any specific recommendations about other experimental paradigms and participant populations. Moreover, different filter settings may be optimal for different scoring methods (e.g., mean amplitude vs. peak amplitude vs. peak latency).

Guanghui Zhang, David Garrett, and I spent the last year focusing on this issue. First we developed a general method that can be used to determine the optimal filter settings for a given dataset and scoring method (see this paper). Then we applied this method to the ERP CORE data to determine the optimal filter settings for the N170, MMN, P3b, N400, N2pc, LRP, and ERN components in neurotypical young adults (see this paper and the table above).

If you are doing research with these components (or similar components) in neurotypical young adults, you can simply use the filter settings that we identified. If you are using a very different paradigm or testing a very different subject population, you can apply our method to your own data to find the optimal settings. We added some new tools to ERPLAB Toolbox to make this easier.

One thing that we discovered was that our old recommendation of 0.1–30 Hz does a good job of avoiding filter artifacts but is overly conservative for some components. For example, we can raise the low end to 0.5 Hz when measuring N2pc and MMN amplitudes, which gets rid of more noise without producing problematic waveform distortions. And we can go all the way up to 0.9 Hz for the N170 component. However, later/slower components like P3b and N400 require lower cutoffs (no higher than 0.2 Hz).

You might be wondering how we defined the “optimal” filter settings. At one level, the answer is simple: The optimal filter is the one that maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio without producing too much waveform distortion. The complexities arise in quantifying the signal-to-noise ratio, quantifying the waveform distortion, and deciding how much waveform distortion is “too much”. We believe we have found reasonably straightforward and practical solutions to these problems, which you can read about in the published papers.

articles.title: Working Through Representation: Malleable Workspaces for Human-Agent Knowledge Work
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30893v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative AI supports knowledge work, yet conversational histories may not capture the evolving organization that guides subsequent action. We introduce the Malleable Workspace, a conceptual model of how humans and agents form and revise a Work Representation and use its organization to advance work within a wider Work Environment. We developed it iteratively through conceptual analysis, comparison of 58 papers, and the construction and three-month longitudinal study of MalleableSpace with seven experienced agent users. Systems varied in what they represented as units and relations. System-assembled context was common; more systems supported local incorporation of agent outputs than reorganization, and fewer supported consequential agent-driven changes beyond the representation. The field study showed how representational roles and organization developed in use. These observations refined the model's account of how representation-grounded action depends on and can change the Work Environment. We contribute a conceptual and analytic foundation for representation-centered human--agent design.
articles.author: Nan Chen, Long Ling, Luna K. Qiu, Zilong Wang, Yuqing Yang

articles.title: ABRA: Agent-Bound UI for Human-Agent Communication beyond Chat with Reusable Views
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30780v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents can create rich representations, yet these representations are rarely used as a medium for expressing user intent. We present Agent-Bound UI, an interaction model that separates reusable interaction structures from task-specific meanings. Agents bind task-specific meanings to interactions in reusable views and publish the resulting bindings as shared state, enabling humans and agents to understand and act on shared surfaces whose meanings vary across tasks. We implement ABRA, a framework-agnostic prototype of Agent-Bound UI, in which users and agents collaborate through chat and shared interactive canvases. We demonstrate ABRA through a representative use case and evaluate four LLM-backed agents on canvas authoring, owner-side consequence resolution, and cross-agent invocation. The code and demo video are available at https://github.com/megagonlabs/abra.
articles.author: Seon Gyeom Kim, Hannah Kim

articles.title: Abstract Priorities, Concrete Rewards: How Stated Preferences Relate to What People Reward in AI Responses
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30763v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI assistants built on large language models (LLMs) are trained on human feedback and increasingly personalized to users' stated preferences. Yet how closely these preferences reflect what people reward in responses remains unclear. We compare stated and revealed preferences in the public PRISM dataset, in which 1,396 participants reported how much seven response attributes mattered to them and then rated 29,347 responses from 21 LLMs. Among responses to the same prompt, features the survey never asked about, such as response length, formatting and refusal language, were at least as strongly associated with ratings as text proxies of the surveyed attributes. Whether stated priorities matched ratings depended on how attributes were measured: participants who prioritized an attribute favoured responses from models that others perceived as strong on it, but not responses that scored higher on text proxies for it. Written feedback was more telling: participants who asked for shorter answers, even in earlier conversations, gave length less weight in their ratings, and those asking for longer answers gave it more. Their relative priorities over the surveyed attributes, however, did not predict this weight. Reasons given for choices reflected perceived attributes more than measured features. Participants also differed stably in how much they weighted several concrete features, especially length, but with a median of 6 conversations per participant, these weights were estimated poorly. The largest gain from personal information in predicting held-out choices was 0.13 percentage points, compared with 1.11 for a stronger pooled model. Stated priorities thus track perceived attributes of AI responses but say little about the concrete features that ratings reward, a distinction that matters for preference elicitation and AI personalization.
articles.author: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu

articles.title: Do We Need to "Be There" to Say Goodbye? Comparing Participatory Agency and Spatial Presence Across Digital Farewell Formats
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30734v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Digitally mediated attachment is increasingly common, yet the mechanisms of symbolic closure in hybrid physical--digital relationships remain underexplored. We address an XR design question: how different mediated farewell formats relate to perceived symbolic closure, spatial presence, and bereavement-related emotional intensity. Using "cloud petting" as a controlled proxy of digitally mediated attachment, we compare three farewell formats: (1) lightweight social messaging, (2) a revisitable web memorial, and (3) immersive VR ritual participation. These formats differ in symbolic participation, spatial presence, and sensorimotor ritual enactment. In a mixed-methods study ($N=45$), Website and VR showed significantly higher perceived symbolic closure than Messaging, while the present sample did not detect a significant closure advantage for VR over Website. VR was also associated with significantly stronger grief-related responses on the Pet Bereavement Questionnaire, whereas negative-affect change measured by the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule did not differ significantly across modalities. This pattern motivates a preliminary, exploratory, mechanism-level Agency-Amplification account: formats supporting structured farewell participation were associated with higher perceived closure, whereas the VR format, combining technical immersion, spatial presence, and sensorimotor ritual enactment, was associated with stronger loss-oriented emotional processing. Because the formats also bundled differences in participation, revisitation, technical immersion, and spatial presence, the study provides preliminary design guidance without isolating the causal contribution of any single feature.
articles.author: Chan In Sio, Alex Mann, Qian Ming Jia, Lik-Hang Lee

articles.title: Big World, Little Me: Comparing a First-Person VR Walkthrough Video and Static Slides for Communicating Height-Related Accessibility Barriers
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30731v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: People with dwarfism and other forms of short stature may encounter barriers created by fixed-height environments and discriminatory social assumptions. This paper evaluates Big World, Little Me, a 10 min 52 s first-person walkthrough recorded from a Unity-based VR environment. The narrative depicts domestic reachability, public-transport, and employment barriers. In a non-randomised between-subjects study, 100 participants aged 15--48 years viewed either the fixed-duration audiovisual walkthrough or a silent, self-paced 27-slide presentation representing the same principal events. Narrative engagement was higher for the walkthrough ($M=5.54$, $SD=0.51$) than for the slides ($M=4.24$, $SD=0.73$), mean difference $=1.30$, 95% CI [1.05, 1.55], Hedges' $g=2.05$, $p<.001$. State empathy was also higher for the walkthrough ($M=3.15$, $SD=0.33$) than for the slides ($M=2.21$, $SD=0.60$), mean difference $=0.94$, 95% CI [0.74, 1.13], Hedges' $g=1.91$, $p<.001$. Exploratory supportive-intention ratings increased more in the walkthrough condition than in the slide condition. Participants also rated the walkthrough as more dynamic, continuous, spatially clear, and information-rich. The findings indicate stronger immediate responses to the complete walkthrough format, but do not isolate the effects of motion, continuity, pacing, information quantity, or participant control. The walkthrough should be understood as screen-based VR-authored media rather than immersive VR or a reproduction of lived experience.
articles.author: Chan In Sio, Alex Mann, Qian Ming Jia, Xuecheng Guo, Yan Zhuo, Xinyu Ning, Kaikuo Liao, Lik-Hang Lee

articles.title: Impacts of generative AI skill development on academic adaptation and learning outcomes among university students
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30599v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding how university students perceive the development of their generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) skills over time can clarify how GenAI use relates to learning and academic outcomes. This study examined perceived skill-development trajectories, changes in learning practices, and associated academic gains using a retrospective questionnaire with 313 analyzed responses and interviews with 18 students across subject areas. Descriptive and comparative analyses and exploratory structural equation modeling (SEM) were integrated with thematic analysis. Perceived developmental trajectories were heterogeneous: 34.2% of students reported rapid early improvement followed by a plateau, 28.4% steady improvement, and 21.1% delayed acceleration. Development was also uneven across skills, with improvement in evaluating GenAI outputs perceived as more challenging; assignments were the most frequently selected driver of skill growth. Interviews further indicated increasingly specific prompting, tailored verification, and selective delegation, although some students reported stable routines, dependence, skipped reasoning, or improvements attributable partly to better GenAI tools. Academic gains were reported more often for assignments than for examinations. The SEM indicated a positive indirect association between perceived skill growth and academic gains through adaptation of assignment processes, whereas academic gains did not clearly differ across developmental trajectory groups after multiplicity correction. The findings suggest that perceived GenAI skill development varies in both trajectory and skill domain and is associated with changes in learning practices and differentiated academic benefits.
articles.author: Lei Fan, Fangxue Liu

articles.title: Beyond Better Ideas: How Human-AI Collaboration Shapes Scientific Ideas and Human Perceptions
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30568v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI increasingly becomes a collaborator in scientific research, its impact may extend beyond improving ideas to reshaping how they are evaluated, attributed, and perceived by humans. Yet existing research has largely examined these dimensions in isolation. We present a unified empirical study of Human-AI scientific ideation, investigating two complementary perspectives: i) how AI collaboration shapes scientific ideas and their evaluation, and ii) how firsthand collaboration reshapes human perceptions of AI. Through a shared experimental setting involving Human-AI and Human-Human research teams, human and LLM evaluators, collaboration-provenance analysis, and participant surveys, we uncover several counterintuitive findings. First, AI collaboration shows no significant advantage in human-evaluated idea quality, while iterative revision consistently improves quality. Second, AI judges can approximate human scores yet disagree on idea rankings; notably, an AI judge favors AI-assisted proposals without a corresponding advantage in human evaluations. Third, collaboration provenance remains only partially detectable, revealing substantial overlap between Human-AI and Human-Human scientific outputs. Finally, firsthand AI collaboration is associated with greater perceived usefulness but smaller efficiency gains than expected, suggesting a nuanced recalibration of human expectations. Overall, our findings challenge the notion that AI's value in scientific ideation lies primarily in producing better ideas, revealing instead its broader influence on scientific creation, evaluation, attribution, and human perceptions.
articles.author: Qian Chen, Saatvik Pradhan, Janice Ahn, Berk Atil, Angkai Li, Shijie Lu, Nobin Sarwar, Michael Ulis, Ruyuan Wan, Wenpeng Yin

articles.title: Atlas: Making Sense of Long Horizon Agent Trajectories
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30548v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents can now search literature, generate hypotheses, analyze datasets, and run experiments at a scale difficult for researchers to match. Yet scaling scientific execution does not automatically scale researchers' ability to make sense of what agents produce. When researchers return to a long-horizon run, they must evaluate work they did not monitor: what the agent produced, which decisions shaped those outputs, and whether those decisions served the research goal. We frame this post-run sensemaking as a representation problem across three linked levels: goal, decision, and artifact. From this framework we developed Atlas, an agentic workspace with a trajectory tree, which renders the run as a branching structure showing what the agent chose and set aside, and artifact projections over six representations. In a within-subjects study (N=14), participants reported higher decision transparency, artifact sensemaking, and goal connection with Atlas than with a standard baseline, together with substantially lower subjective workload.
articles.author: Sangho Suh, Joseph Chee Chang, Pao Siangliulue, Amy X. Zhang, Matt Latzke, Jonathan Bragg, Doug Downey, Daniel S. Weld

articles.title: Exploring spatial configuration and group familiarity when co-watching 360-degree stories in social virtual reality
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30353v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While traditional cinematic viewing is often characterized as a social experience, engaging with immersive stories is predominantly researched as an individual activity. This mismatch becomes increasingly problematic in social virtual reality (VR), where features designed for typical social activities (e.g., virtual locomotion, spatial and social context) can become meaningful levers for shaping the user experience. To address our limited understanding of these effects, we conducted three exploratory experiments (N$_1$=109, N$_2$=116, N$_3$=88) examining how spatial boundary type, size of allocated personal space, and group familiarity influence co-watching 360-degree stories in social VR. Results shows that small communal spatial boundaries heightened social presence towards others compared to individual boundaries, but also increased mental demand. Reducing the size of the personal spatial boundary increased social presence towards others but also increased disorientation and frustration. Finally, participants with higher group familiarity reported stronger attentional focus on the story, as well as higher spatial presence and social presence towards story characters, but also reported greater physical and perceptual demand. We discuss systematic tradeoffs between engagement and cognitive effort, and suggest practical guidelines for designing shared immersive narrative experiences.
articles.author: Portia Wang, Monique Santoso, Yujie Tao, Jeremy Bailenson

articles.title: Measuring undergraduate students' reliance on generative AI during problem-solving: Scale development and validation
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30195v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliance on AI describes the behavioral patterns of when and how individuals depend on AI suggestions, and appropriate reliance patterns are necessary to achieve effective human-AI collaboration. Traditional measures often link reliance to decision-making outcomes, which may not be suitable for complex problem-solving tasks where outcomes are not binary (i.e., correct or incorrect) or immediately clear. Therefore, this study aims to develop a scale to measure undergraduate students' behaviors of using Generative AI during problem-solving tasks without directly linking them to specific outcomes. We conducted an exploratory factor analysis on 800 responses collected after students finished one problem-solving activity, which revealed four distinct factors: reflective use, cautious use, thoughtless use, and collaborative use. The overall scale has reached sufficient internal reliability (Cronbach's alpha = .84). Two confirmatory factor analyses (CFAs) were conducted to validate the factors using the remaining 730 responses from this activity and 1,173 responses from another problem-solving activity. CFA indices showed adequate model fit for data from both problem-solving tasks, suggesting that the scale can be applied to various human-AI problem-solving tasks. This study offers a validated scale to measure students' reliance behaviors in different human-AI problem-solving activities and provides implications for educators to responsively integrate Generative AI in higher education.
articles.author: Chenyu Hou, Gaoxia Zhu, Vidya Sudarshan, Fun Siong Lim, Yew Soon Ong

articles.title: A Formalizable Proof of the No-Supervenience Theorem: A Diagonal Limitation on the Viability of Physicalist Theories of Consciousness
articles.content:
arXiv:2307.10178v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The no-supervenience theorem limits the capacity of physicalist theories to provide a comprehensive account of human consciousness. The proof of the theorem is difficult to formalize because it relies on both alethic and epistemic notions of possibility. This article outlines a formalizable proof using predicate modal logic in which the epistemic inferences are expressed in terms of an existing mathematical formalism, the inference device (Wolpert, 2008). The resulting proof shows definitely that any physicalist theory which describes a self-aware, intelligent system must be internally inconsistent.
articles.author: Cathy M Reason

articles.title: Dynamics of random recurrent neural networks: colored noise and sublinear activations
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.31575v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the dynamics of recurrent neural networks with random couplings, sublinear odd activation functions, and temporally correlated noise. Using large N methods, we determine stationary correlations and distinguish the loss of local linear stability from the onset of chaos, characterized by a positive largest Lyapunov exponent. These thresholds delimit an intermediate regime in which local instability coexists with asymptotic stability under a common noise history. Their separation depends on both the noise correlation time and the asymptotic growth of the activation function. We show that internal noise with any finite correlation time cuts off the divergence of the network's intrinsic correlation time tau_corr at the edge of chaos; it exhibits a critical scaling tau_{corr,max} propto 1/sqrt{D_0}, where D_0 is the integrated noise strength. Static random input instead produces coincident thresholds and a divergent correlation time. We also calculate the frequency-dependent participation dimension from a four-point correlation function. Its zero-frequency value is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the network correlation time, predicting a smooth minimum at the weak-noise chaos threshold. Numerical simulations support the large-network predictions and reveal appreciable finite-size effects.
articles.author: German Mato, Facundo Rigatuso, Gonzalo Torroba

articles.title: Music Between Two Minds: Individual Signatures, Shared States, and the Emergence of Creative Interaction
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.31131v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Some of the most valued forms of human creativity arise between people-in conversation, collaboration, and improvised music-yet how two minds jointly regulate the flow of novelty in real time remains unknown. Here we examined the information dynamics of interpersonal improvisation using 986 professional jazz improvisations. Pitch-based fluctuations of uncertainty and surprise behaved as signatures of individual identity: the two partners differed within 90% of takes, performers were identifiable from single solos and the separation between partners persisted undiminished across turns and takes. Rhythm-based fluctuations showed the reverse organization: partners were statistically indistinguishable within a take yet shifted together from take to take, and this shared state drifted gradually as each performance progressed, with each performer moving away from their own past at the same rate as from their partner's. Beyond joint drift, solo hand-offs revealed turn-by-turn complementarity: when one performer exceeded their own average surprise in the predictive dynamics of improvisation, the partner's next solo fell below their own, in both pitch and rhythm and in all duos. Improvising pairs thus neither fuse into one system nor remain two independent ones: they preserve individual melodic voices while sharing a rhythmic state, within which moment-to-moment push-pull continually rebalances their interaction. Individuality and togetherness thus coexist, carried by different musical dimensions, a measurable organization of creativity that emerges between minds.
articles.author: Tatsuya Daikoku, Risa Kobayashi, Rina Tabuchi, Yoshia Abe, Yasuo Kuniyoshi

articles.title: Gate-Based Feature Importance in Simulation-Based Inference for EEG: A Cautionary Tale
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30364v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) provides a powerful way to fit mechanistic models to data, but offers little insight into which information in the data shapes the inferred parameter values. It could therefore benefit from robust and inexpensive interpretability methods. Learned weighting mechanisms such as feature gates provide a potential route to low-cost interpretability, although their interpretation assumes that predictive training reveals which inputs drive performance. We examined this assumption in a computational neuroscience setting, where neural posterior estimation (NPE) is used to infer four physiological parameters of a dynamical model of interacting neuronal populations (Jansen-Rit). We tested whether the learned gate weights captured feature importance by comparing them with a retrain-based ablation benchmark, in which each feature was removed in turn and the NPE retrained. We considered two jointly trained gates: independent sigmoid weights and competing softmax weights. If these reliably reflect feature importance, they should align with the ablation-based estimates. Across nine independent training seeds, however, gate-based and ablation-based importance were negatively correlated (Spearman's rho approximately -0.61 for sigmoid gating and -0.56 for softmax gating). The feature that ablation identified as most important, total signal power, was among the features the gate down-weighted most, despite gating costing negligible predictive accuracy. These results extend a pattern previously documented for attention mechanisms in natural language processing and for explainability methods in electroencephalography (EEG) deep learning to the simulation-based inference setting, and suggest caution when interpreting learned gate weights as measures of causal feature importance in scientific machine-learning pipelines.
articles.author: Shrivatsa Deshmukh, Sasha Brenner, Thomas R. Kn\"osche, Nico Scherf

articles.title: The medium is the message: How neurometabolic entanglement generates conscious experience
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30217v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most neuroscientific accounts of consciousness assume that conscious experience is constituted by the information conveyed between neurons. The physical-chemical details of the metabolic and physiological processes that convey this information are correspondingly presumed to be relevant only insofar as they support the organization of information processes. We describe an alternative perspective that denies this presumed independence of the processing of neural information and the metabolic-physiological details of these processes. We call this alternative paradigm the theory of neuro-metabolic entanglement (NME). NME proposes that mental experience exemplifies the inseparability of the organization of neural information processes from the constraints imposed by the material-energetic properties of the neural medium itself. Central to this account is a recursive, M\"obius-like loop of neural connections that entangles patterns of forebrain information processing with midbrain regulatory systems that modulate forebrain metabolism. This enables patterns of neural activity to indirectly modify the global distribution of metabolic resources underlying these information processes. It also constitutes a bottleneck that integrates diverse neural processes into an adaptively relevant unitary experience organized in terms of the global redistribution of metabolic support. Computational models of neural function cannot treat energy supply as a fixed background parameter; our proposed M\"obius-like loop of neuro-metabolic entanglement offers a framework for future models in which neural activity is dynamically and recursively modulated by the network's own metabolism. Recognizing this entanglement is a first step toward dissolving the explanatory gap highlighted by the so-called "hard problem" of consciousness.
articles.author: Terrence W. Deacon, Miguel Garcia-Valdecasas, Michael Jacob
